utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is the 26th of November 2007. My greetings to the representatives of the OTP, they are all here. The same for the Defence counsel, the accused and all the people assisting us in our work. As you know, today we are going to have a witness who is to testify over two days. On Wednesday and Thursday, we'll start at 8.00 in the morning, since we are going to have a video conference as well as a witness who is coming for the admission of a single document, so he should be pretty short. Before proceeding, I'll give the floor to the Deputy Registrar -- to the registrar for some IC numbers, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness EA. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 722; the list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 723; the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 724; the list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 725; while the list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 726. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I wanted to point out to the parties that the Trial Chamber issued several decisions last week. They were filed and I invite you to read them. There is a major one, that was the second order modifying the schedule. You may know it, you may not; the Trial Chamber decided that the Prosecution case would finish on the 24th of January 2008. The 98 bis arguments will be submitted from the 28th of January to the 6th of February 2008. Each of the accused will have three hours to submit their arguments. As to the Prosecution, they will have nine hours and the Trial Chamber said that there would be no rejoinder, following which, further to 65 ter G rule, the lists will be filed at the latest the 3rd of March 2008. As to the pre-Defence case conference, it will be on the 13th of March 2008. It is aimed, as you know, to fix the number of witnesses and the time for each of the witnesses. As to the beginning of the Defence case, it will take place on the 17th of March 2008. So please read the order which was drafted in French but you should receive the translation in English very shortly. Let us move for -- to private session for a few moments, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution will have three hours. The Defence three and a half hours. Mr. Pusic will have one hour and the other Defence teams 30 minutes each. Of course, you're free to give away some of your time, as you please. But we thought that Mr. Pusic's team should have one hour for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Let me check that you can hear me. If you hear me, say so, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, before you read out the solemn declaration, please state your first name, family name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Amor Masovic. I was born on the 29th of November 1955 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you got a current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At present, I am one of the three directors of the institute for missing persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the vice presiding person of the commission for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you had an opportunity to testify before a national or international court as to the events that took place in your country or is this the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified in two cases before this Tribunal, in 2001, from the 20th to the 22nd of March, and from the 24th to the 25th of September, and I have also testified on a number of occasions before the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina for war crimes committed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and before the cantonal courts in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in front of the district court and the council for war crimes in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So I see that you've testified on several occasions, including twice before this Tribunal. In which cases, could you tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In March 2001, the -- my testimony was in the trial of the Prosecutor versus Milorad Krnojelac and in September, unless I'm much mistaken, of that same year it was the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic, those two trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read out the solemn declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please sit down. Let me provide some information regarding the way these two hearing days are going to unfold, briefly, because you already are experienced when it comes to testifying before this Tribunal. So you will be first put questions by Mr. Stringer, based on documents he's going to submit to you. I suppose you have seen the documents together with Mr. Stringer, at least this weekend. Following which and this should take the whole day today, tomorrow or perhaps already early -- later this afternoon you will have cross-examination by several counsel, as you see here today, but each Defence team represents a -- one accused and they each will put questions to you in cross-examination. You have four judges before you. They, too, can ask questions. Generally speaking, we put our questions once the examination-in-chief and cross-examination have taken place, but since you may have a document in front of you we may like to put questions at that time rather than look for the document later. And if we do so, we put follow-up questions as we call them. As you know, we have breaks every 90 minutes and we break for 20 minutes. If at any time you do not feel well, just tell us so. If you wish to ask a question of the Judges, do not hesitate either. Raise your hand. If you do not understand a question, ask the person putting it to reformulate, to rephrase it. So this is how the testimony is going to take place. Let me also tell you that depending on the kind of questions and answers provided, if at any point in time your answer is likely to incriminate you because at the time you had certain functions, you may decide or say that you do not want to answer the question. This is something really quite out of the ordinary. We've never come across such a situation but if it were to arise, the question -- the Trial Chamber may ask you to answer the question all the same. Let me give the floor to the OTP for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon to you and to Your Honours, counsel and to all of the other people around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Masovic, welcome.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In the introduction that you've already given in response to the questions from the President, you indicated that currently you are working and associated with the Institute for Missing Persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm one of the three directors of the institute, and the vice presiding officer of the federal commission, that is to say the commission of one of the two Bosnia-Herzegovinian entities for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you a couple of questions about those two commissions, both the state-level Institute for Missing Persons, and then also the federal or the federation level commission that you've just mentioned. Can you just perhaps tell the Judges what are these two entities, what are the differences between them and most importantly, what are the responsibilities and the mandates of these two commissions that you're associated with?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The Dayton Accords provided for the existence of two entities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Federation and Republika Srpska. The governments of both these two entities, at the beginning of 1996, passed decisions on the establishment of commissions for the tracing of missing persons. That was a necessity because Bosnia and Herzegovina was faced with a large number of missing persons that went missing during the aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina. The number reached about 30.000, in fact. So as on the basis of the peace agreement reached in Dayton, it was decided to help resolve the problem of missing persons. The governments took the decision or made decisions to form the commissions. The commission established by the then-government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was called the State Commission for the Tracing of Missing Persons. And I was appointed as its president, and I remained in that position right up until the beginning of last year when it ceased to exist, when that state commission ceased to exist. At the same time, the Government of Republika Srpska formed its own commission for missing persons, or the tracing of missing persons, with headquarters in Banja Luka. The mandate of those two commissions was in a way the same, but it also differed. It was the same in the sense that both commissions had the task of tracing and looking for missing persons, missing persons applies to both missing civilians and missing soldiers who went missing in military operations as well as persons that went missing and came from the territories of other states, especially the neighbouring states. That is to say, Serbia and Montenegro and at the time the Republic of Croatia, persons who went missing on the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, the difference in the mandates, the basic difference between these two submissions, the state commission whose president I was and the commission of Republika Srpska lay in the following. The state commission tried, it did not always succeed, but it did try, not to differentiate and make any difference between the ethnic -- ethnicities of the missing persons whereas the commission of Republika Srpska engaged in the tracing of missing Serbs. The state commission tried to encompass everybody during their exhumations or investigations right up to the month of June or July 1996, to look for all missing persons, when, at that time, in Banja Luka, an agreement was signed on inter-ethnic exhumations, which allowed these two commissions the right to conduct exhumations of mass graves, individual graves or whatever, on the territory of the other entity. In 1997, the federal commission for missing persons was established which de jure was formed in 1997, but de facto started working sometime later. That is to say, roughly at around the year 2000, when the government of the federation started to finance it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And let me just jump in at this point because I want to clarify, the federal commission that you've just mentioned, formed in 1997, this then would be a commission comprised of representatives of the Croat and the Muslim or Bosniak communities then in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then again getting back to the institute for missing persons which you are associated with also at this time, it's my understanding that this institute for missing persons or MPI, as it's called, is a more recently established entity under the law at the state level of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it is intended then to bring together representatives of the three groups or nations as well as the international commission for missing persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The agreement on co-financing of the institute that you're referring to was signed between the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the council of ministers, and the representatives of the international commission for tracing missing persons on the 30th of August 2005. And since it was an international agreement, what was needed was that it be ratified by the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that followed several months later. I think that took place on the 28th of November 2005, and from that day on, from November 2005, up to the present day, the institute has been in existence, the institute for tracing missing persons, it has the directors, the supervisory board, executive board, it still does not have the necessary employees but we expect to have a full staff once the papers and documents of the institute are passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And is it correct to say, Mr. Masovic, that in one capacity or another, you've been directly involved at a high level with the commissions responsible for locating and identifying missing persons in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the years since the conflict ended in 1995?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I'm the president of the commission at state level. I am the deputy chairperson of the federal commission, dating back to 1997. And I'm one of the three directors of the institute for tracing missing persons since March 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you're also a member, currently, of the federation parliament in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. I'm a deputy in one of the two houses of the federation of the parliament of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to take you back, then, just to briefly describe for the Trial Chamber the role that you played prior to the end of the conflict in respect of prisoners of war, prisoner exchange and attempts to locate missing persons at that time before the conflict ended. Were you involved in that and if you could tell us a bit about the extent of your involvement?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: When the aggression against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina started, that is to say, already in April 1992, the then-Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina formed a commission which was called the state commission for the exchange of prisoners of war and persons who have been deprived of liberty, and records of persons who were killed, wounded or missing. And I joined that commission in the second half of August 1992, and for a time I was a member of that commission, and for a time I was also the vice-president of the commission, and in the latter stage, after the Dayton Accords, I was the acting president of that state commission. The commission's mandate emanated from its title. Well, it did what its title said. It was in charge of seeing that as many prisoners of war as possible or civilian persons who were in detention in enemy camps or prisons be freed through the process of exchange, and the other essential task of the commission was to make records of all those who had been killed, wounded or missing, persons killed, wounded or missing during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can we say that during -- that Sarajevo is your home and that this is the place where you were based and that you worked from during the entire time of the conflict and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Throughout all that time, Sarajevo was also the seat of all these commissions, both during the war and after the war, save for the commission that I spoke about which was seated in Banja Luka, the commission for the missing persons of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in directing your attention now to the summer and to the fall, the autumn, of 1993, then, is that when you became involved yourself in respect of prisoner exchange, prisoners of war issues, as between the Armija and the HVO, the Muslims and the Croats, in that conflict?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I was not directly involved in the exchanges but one may say I was involved indirectly by receiving information from the commissions that were part of the state commissions that were called district commission for exchanges. They would inform me about the exchanges that had been undertaken at the local levels between the BiH army and the Croatian Defence Council, and this went on up to autumn 1993 approximately, and after that, I became directly involved in the process of liberating prisoners which involved the BiH army and the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So that prior then to the autumn of 1993, you were focused primarily or perhaps even exclusively on prisoner issues in respect of the conflict with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Berislav Pusic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there is a mistake in the transcript. The gentleman said that he occasionally received information, not all the time. Occasionally he would receive information from the district commissions up to autumn 1993, and it was recorded that he received information all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that's what is reported at least in the English transcripts. I'm looking at line 1 of page 15 where it simply indicates the witness said that he was involved indirectly by receiving information from the commissions. I don't know that the witness said that he received information all the time. I don't think it's a very important point but I could ask the witness to clarify that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I thought you were going to ask that question. Since you haven't I'm going to do that myself. Sir, we understand that as of the month of August 1992 you were in charge of taking care of prisoner exchanges in Sarajevo but I'm interested in this. Before August 1992, what were you doing? How come you were appointed to that position? What were you doing before August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before August 1992, I was attorney at law in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were a lawyer, attorney at law and who appointed you in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, in the month of August, I was appointed as a member of the state commission, and the members were appointed by the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just before the intervention, I --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: What was your question? You asked me whether I knew Mr. Berislav Pusic and my answer to that is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us when you first met Mr. Pusic personally?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I first met him in Medjugorje in the headquarters of the Spanish Battalion, the then protection forces also known as UNPROFOR, on the 29th of December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. In front of you you have a binder of exhibits and you and I have had an opportunity to go through most of these previously. Let me direct you to Exhibit 7417. P 07417. Now, sir, this is a report dated the 31st of December 1993. It appears to be over the signature or I should say over the name of Mr. Pusic, and it's referring to a meeting that you had with him on the 29th of December. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, the circumstances that led to this meeting and what you remember about the meeting, why it is at this point that you were meeting with Mr. Pusic in Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The circumstances that led to my departure from Medjugorje are partly clear from the document that I have before me. After the negotiations or various attempts at negotiations about the exchange of prisoners of war at local level, and when I say local level, I mean one part of Herzegovina comprising Mostar, Jablanica, Prozor, Konjic, and Capljina, there was a stalemate in the negotiations at the local level. In the meantime, three sticking points surfaced in the relations between the BiH army and the Croatian Defence Council. In addition to the ongoing topical subject, at least when it came to the BiH army, and that was the issue of camps, i.e., prisons, in the territory under the control of the HVO. Therefore, there were the three following topics that arose which were a direct cause of my departure for Medjugorje: The first one was the 13 imprisoned members of the BiH army who were captured on the 10th of May 1993 in a building popularly known as Vranica building, and the footage of that event and their appearance before the cameras of the Croatian television were not only in the region but also across the world, and this is what resulted in a very electrified atmosphere in the territory of Mostar and the territory under the control of the BiH army because the parents of these soldiers wanted the problem to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I'm hearing you talk and I'm also listening to the interpretation, and although the interpreters haven't said anything yet it's possible that it would assist them if you could try to speak a little more slowly so that they can be sure to capture all of your words and put them into the languages that we are all listening in here. So I apologise for cutting you off there. You were talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'd like to say something. Mr. Masovic, when I asked the question, I learned that you were attorney at law and you are now an MP so you know what you are talking about. The prosecutor presented to you a document. It is mentioned in English, "exchange of detainees". And whilst I was listening to you, I heard you say, "prisoners of war". This is what I want to know: When you mention the exchange of prisoners, are we speaking about military detainees, military prisoners, or military and civilian prisoners? Because in this document, at least in the translation in English, which may not be absolutely faithful to the original, it is indicated as being the Commission for Exchange of Detainees and Other Persons. Therefore I suppose the other persons are civilians. So when you're answering the question put to you, do make a distinction, please, between prisoners of war, who generally are military personnel that have been captured, and those who have a civilian status so that we know where we are going. You have the floor again, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try to bear that in mind myself in the questions that I'm asking, although it is my intention to explore this issue in greater detail with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, now that we have this little bit of a break because you were giving us a lot of information and so I'd like to break down a little bit what it is that we have so far in respect of this exhibit, 7417. You had indicated first of all, I believe, that there had been negotiations taking place at a lower level or at a different level which had reached a sticking point, I think was at least the words I got in English. And if you could just very briefly amplify on that, the extent to which negotiations and communications had been taking place prior to your involvement in the Mostar area in respect of prisoner exchange, as far as you knew, who was doing the talking on the side of the Armija or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, if you will allow me, Your Honours, I would like to go back to what you said about the status of prisoners of war. In my further testimony, when I speak about prisoners or prisoners of war, I'm always going to imply both categories, both the prisoners in terms of the Third Geneva Conventions and civilians in terms of the Fourth Geneva Conventions, given the fact that both groups were in the camps, in the prisons, sometimes they shared or often they shared the same rooms, and they were treated the same way by the prison or camp authorities. All of the negotiations from the beginning of April 1992 to the Dayton peace accords that took place and that I was involved in, be it with the Serb side or the Croatian side, always involved both categories of prisoners, to put it that way. In other words, as I provide my further answers when I say prisoners, I will imply both categories. And now, as far as the prosecutor's question is concerned, I said in the introduction to my testimony that my first immediate contact with regard to the exchanges of prisoners from the territory of Herzegovina took place on the 19th of October 1993. I was a member of a mixed delegation consisting of governmental and non-governmental officials, namely the then-Minister of External Affairs, Mr. Silajdzic, Mr. Ivo Komsic, Mr. Andjelovic who was a priest, and I represented a local level. There was another representative of a commission from Konjic. We discussed the exchange of prisoners between Herzegovina and Konjic. That exchange comprised a large number of people, I believe around 800 prisoners altogether were liberated on that occasion, on the 19th of October 1993. In the negotiations on the Croatian side, there were members of the HVO from Konjic, nobody from Mostar. They were rather all from Konjic. On that occasion, the army released 309 prisoners from Konjic and the HVO released approximately 550 people from Herzegovina and from two prisons in the vicinity of Konjic including the so-called Tuzla delegation, a delegation consisting of nine civilians, among whom was also a Muslim mufti from Tuzla, Mr. Husein Efendi Kavazovic. I will go back now to the reasons for my departure to Medjugorje because I-- I'll give only one reason which was the Vranica group. The second reason for my --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I wanted to get back because you may have misunderstood my last question so perhaps I could just direct your attention to the third paragraph of the document that's in front of you there, in which Mr. Pusic is writing that the republican commission of the ABiH have not been fully informed. He's saying that there is another meeting that is scheduled in shortly after beginning of January and so I just wanted to ask you briefly again, this indicates that there had been some negotiations between Mr. Pusic and others prior to your involvement. And I just wanted to ask you if that is -- corresponds to what you said earlier about negotiations in the Mostar area that had been taking place at a lower level with Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. The third paragraph is correct. The negotiations took place at the local level, between the east and west part of Mostar. They were partly successful. They resulted in some exchanges of prisoners, some handovers of the fallen soldiers or civilians, up to the moment of the blockade which was the reason for my going to Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in terms of issues that resulted in this blockade or this -- the sticking points, as you were mentioning, one of which, the first one, you've already described and we will be talking about it in much greater detail, the issue of the Vranica, the soldiers captured at the Vranica building, is -- well, why don't you tell us, there were two others, I believe, that you wanted to tell us and if you could just indicate for the Trial Chamber briefly what were the other two issues that were causing this blockade in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The second reason for the stalemate was the capturing of between 70 and 73, the figures differ, of members of the HVO and several members of the Croatian army in the Herzegovina region. They were kept in the Armija's prison in the eastern part of Mostar. The Croatian side, i.e., the Croatian Defence Council, was very interested in their release. However, in a certain way, all further negotiations about the release of these men were stipulated from the Eastern Mostar, i.e., they depended on the information about the destiny of the Vranica prisoners, namely the families of those prisoners put a lot of pressure on the command of the 4th Corps of the BiH army to involve those people in the negotiations and to have them released, as they were seen on TV screens. And these families put an ultimatum to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then as I understand it, the issue of any release of the HVO prisoners or HV prisoners from East Mostar was linked or was dependent upon a similar resolution of the issue of the Vranica prisoners? You need to say yes or no for the record.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. At that time, those two issues were mutually dependent, and one depended on the other. The third reason for my departure for Medjugorje was the blockade of two medical helicopters of the BiH army in Medjugorje. Those helicopters were part of the medical corps and their task was to transport the wounded between Zenica and Central Bosnia to Split for treatment there. Or further transfer to third countries for treatment or recovery. These helicopters, as far as I can remember, were grounded by force in Medjugorje and kept there. After that, Croatian families of the 70 Croats who were kept in -- as prisoners in Eastern Mostar blocked those helicopters and the eight-member crews including a nurse, were urgently evacuated to the Spanish Battalion base in Medjugorje. The helicopters were -- remained in a school playground or a plateau, I'm not sure that there was a school in question. And the Croatian families said that they would only allow the helicopters to take off if their family members were liberated from the prison in Eastern Mostar. There was another reason for me to go to Medjugorje and that was the task that I had been given directly from the then-President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic, and the task was to try and establish the lot and release the assistant commander for logistics of the 4th Corps or the -- of the BiH army, Mr. Mirsad Mahmutcehajic whose lot was not known at the time. It was not known whether he was among the living. Also Mr. Zijad Demirovic who was a highly positioned member of the SDA party in Herzegovina. At that time his lot was not known either. So those were the reasons for my going to Medjugorje and participating in the negotiations there on the 29th of December 1993, all the reasons that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It sounds as though, then, all of these -- all four of these reasons that you've described, Vranica, the helicopters, HVO prisoners, Mr. Mahmutcehajic and Demirovic, these were all linked together or had become linked together in one way or another by the sides?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Throughout all these talks, the things got so complicated that all these things depended on each other and were mutually conditioned. You said four reasons. And I would say that the first reason that I said at the beginning was to try and establish the real condition of the total number of prisoners in the camps in Herzegovina and parts of Central Bosnia in which the Croatian Defence Council had its prisons or camps. That was the first and the principal reason, and then there were some particular reasons after that, the four that I mentioned, subsequently. At that meeting in Medjugorje, we also discussed certain individual cases, such as was the case of Mersa Krzic, who had been arrested. She had been the director of the Natron Maglaj company. On the other side, Mr. Sandrk participated in those negotiations and he inquired about the lot of 200 Croats from Bugojno who according to him had been taken away in the direction of Gornji Vakuf, and their lot was not known. He asked me to inform him about the lot of these people. And there were also some other individual cases discussed on that date, on the 29th of December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Let me take you to the next paragraph, then, after the one we were just looking at. This goes a little bit toward the issue or the question raised by the president already. This document indicates, according to Mr. Pusic, that it's necessary or he's asking them to submit a list of the detained persons of the Muslim ethnicity held in prisons "under your control," and this is a document that's being directed to the Tomislav military district, the Rama brigade. Could I ask you just to comment on that issue, the extent to which during this period there were persons of Muslim ethnicity, whether or not civilians or soldiers, who were in the custody of the HVO in these various locations?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to tell you precisely because immediately before the meeting in Medjugorje on the 29th of December 1993, I believe over 3.000 prisoners had been liberated pursuant to an order which was believed to have arrived from Mr. Tudjman, the President of Croatia, and there order was carried out through Mr. Mate Boban, i.e., through the Commission for Exchanges of Prisoners that was run by Mr. Pusic. I believe that by then already 3.000 people had been released and we did not have the exact information about the remainder of the prisoners in the Herzegovina prisons, as well as in some other camps and prisons in Livno, Kaonik, Kiseljak, Kresevo and so on and so forth. I believe that at that time, however, it was believed that some 700-plus prisoners were still kept in the prisons and camps of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me direct you to another exhibit in the binder, sir. It's marked as Exhibit 6929. And Mr. Masovic, this is not a report or a document made by you or one that you would have seen at the time but there are just a couple points in it that I'd like to raise with you. I'm looking about halfway down the first page of the English, the original language version. And this is making reference to a meeting in Medjugorje which doesn't appear that you were present at but it may be that you can comment on some of these issues. There is a reference to Mr. Pusic informing that he was not prepared to accept an all-for-all exchange. Do you see that part? "At the second meeting with the president of the HVO prisoner exchange committee, Mr. Berko Pusic, he informed ECMM that in this instance he was not prepared to accept all-for-all as it would mean HVO releasing 2500 Muslims and receiving only 70 HVO prisoners." And then this continues down a couple lines, makes a reference to the issue of the helicopters, as you've already described, and so recognising that this document is dated just prior to about a month prior to your involvement, 28th of November 1993, I wanted to ask you about two things. First of all, the HVO position, based on you knew it to be and after you did get involved, in respect of all-for-all exchange. What does all-for-all mean?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pusic says that in the document, all-for-all. And all-for-all meant that the ratio of those freed would be drastically -- well, under inverted commas, of course, to the detriment of the Croatian Defence Council. Now, why do I say that? Because in the camps or prisons of the Croatian Defence Council, throughout the time, from the very beginning of the conflict, right up until the end or rather the Washington agreement and after the Washington accords as well, throughout that time, there were mostly civilians there or a far greater number of civilians than there were members of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or in this case members of the BH army. And liberation or setting people free according to the all-for-all principle in certain times would mean for the HVO a ratio of one to ten, for example. That is to say that the HVO had to release ten prisoners, Bosniaks, and for that only one HVO member would be released or one Croat. So that kind of agreement was not to the advantage of the HVO, and Mr. Pusic, not just once but a number of times, at meetings, although sometimes he emphasised that he did wish to have the all-for-all principle in the exchange, in the implementation of these kinds of agreements, the all-for-all ones, there was always some obstruction or some additional conditions laid down which deferred the process or overrode these agreements of all-for-all exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Beginning with your first meeting with Mr. Pusic, then, on the 29th of December 1993, could you give the Trial Chamber in general terms an idea of how many meetings then you had with Mr. Pusic on the issues of prisoner exchange during the time prior to the end of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in November of 1995? I want to break up your testimony between the pre-conflict and the post-conflict period. So this period of time prior to the end of the conflict, how many meetings did you have with Mr. Pusic in respect of prisoner exchange issues?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the signing of the peace agreement for Bosnia and Herzegovina in Dayton or rather in Paris, I think that the number of meetings, there were a number of meetings held to discuss the exchange of prisoners of war or the question of missing persons was dealt with after the Washington agreements and I'm sure there were more than 50 such meetings, and some of them went on for several days, two or even three days. So the meetings were interrupted, then taken up the next day, then they weren't completed the following day but went into the third day. So I think there were more than 50 such meetings in different areas including Medjugorje where they mostly took place. Then they were held in Kiseljak, in Sarajevo, in Gornji Vakuf, Tuzla and I think -- yes, in the post-Dayton period there were some more meetings outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, but after Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was the focus -- can you describe whether there is any change, then, in the focus of the meetings and the discussions you were having with Mr. Pusic at the time the conflict was still taking place versus then after the conflict ended?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: If I wanted to be brief and precise, and to depict the real image for you, so you could understand, in the war period, that is to say up to the signing of the Washington agreements, when the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council were in play, and in the focus of the meetings were living persons. That is to say, POWs, people who were alive, including civilians. Now, in the post-Dayton period or post-Washington period, what they focused on, what we focused on in our meetings were the dead, the missing which were later seen to be dead. They turned out to be dead, not just missing. So during the war we dealt with living people. In the post-war period we dealt with the missing and dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarifying, Mr. President and Your Honours. He keeps talking about the post-war period and he's interchanging between Washington agreement which is the creation of the Federation, and of course the Dayton peace accords signed in Dayton and then after in Paris. Which one does he mean? And again, the indictment stops at a particular point in 1994. Now, unless there is some contextual purposes, I just think we need to be a little more focused and perhaps a little more precise with the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Would you kindly be a little bit clearer in what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, we know that the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims ended with the Washington agreement at the beginning of March 1994. And let's focus on your dealings with Mr. Pusic prior to the Washington agreement and during the couple of months that followed, and I've got some documents to show you that relate to that, and so -- and then we'll talk a bit -- then we'll talk about the issues that follow in respect of the missing persons and dead in the years that followed the Washington agreement. During this period of time, your meetings with Mr. Pusic, prior to and around the time of the Washington agreement, just tell us, based on your observations, what was his title, what was his role, what was his level of responsibility and authority in respect of the prisoner issues?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to tell you what I know about. And what I know about is this: That he was the number one man or the chief of the commission or service for the exchange of prisoners of war and other persons, although already at the time in Medjugorje I learnt that in a way he did some other things too, which had nothing to do with the exchanges and that kind of thing was the evacuation of civilian persons from territories under the control of one armed force to another territory controlled by another force or, rather, BH army territory to HVO territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm rather surprised actually, and I'll tell you why. You said that you met Mr. Pusic for the first time at Medjugorje on 29th December 1993. The conflict between the HVO and the ABiH goes back to September 1993 but before that as well, we know that from the witnesses that have come already from 1992 it's clear that there were conflicts, there were prisoners taken, so given that, you appear to be, number 1, in charge on the Bosnia-Herzegovinian side and then according to what you say, your counterpart Mr. Pusic represented the HVO. How is it that you only met each other in December? That's the particular point that I don't follow. Can you explain that? The conflict therefore goes back actually at least a year in time. In fact rather more than a year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conflict, the mass conflict between the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council started from mid-April 1993. So that's when I met Mr. Pusic for the first time. That is to say six months after the conflict actually began. And I explained in my introduction the reasons for that. The first reason was that up until then, up until my direct contact with Mr. Pusic, things functioned. That is to say, they evolved on a local level in Central Bosnia, Travnik, Zenica, Stari Vitez, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, in Herzegovina, around Mostar, Konjic, Jablanica, Prozor, exchange did take place both of prisoners of war and the bodies of persons who had been killed. So there was no need for me physically to be present at meetings with Mr. Pusic. So that's one reason. The second reason is the following: Sarajevo and that's common knowledge, I believe, was under a complete siege, blockade, on the one hand, and after the conflict with the Croatian Defence Council, Mostar too was completely blocked off. So that every time I had to leave Sarajevo, I would have to rely on assistance given to me by the protection forces because the only way in which I could reach Jablanica, which was under the BH army or to East Mostar under the BH army's control or Medjugorje under the HVO's control, the only way was for me to get into an APC and for the UNPROFOR protection forces to transport me there, which wasn't easy. There were incidents along the way, there were situations where my life was endangered, in these APCs, but their details, I don't know whether they are essential now for me to tell you about them. But six months after the massive conflict between the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council was the first time I physically met Mr. Pusic. I have already said that before my meeting with Mr. Pusic, and that was on the 19th of October 1993, a major exchange took place. I don't know whether Mr. Pusic took part and if so to what extent in this massive exchange but it was agreed upon in Konjic on the territory that was controlled under the BH army, and a Mr. Pusic -- since Mr. Pusic was not directly involved in the negotiations to free more than 800 prisoners, including the Tuzla delegation, with the mufti, Husein Efendi Kavazovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed for your answer which does actually clarify for me that you only met in December 1993. Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, my last question to you, and you've answered it, which was to describe in general terms the role and the responsibilities of Mr. Pusic as you observed them to be based on your dealings during this period just before and just after the Washington agreement. Let me ask you now, based on that experience with Mr. Pusic during this period, and perhaps also based on your experience on the October 1993 release which you've already talked about, could you tell us your observations, conclusions in respect of HVO policy in the taking of prisoners and the release of prisoners, whether they be civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may object at this point, there is a lack of foundation. If -- there are two parts to this question; the first part is the taking of prisoners. Now, I want to know exactly what are we talking about? And secondly, what is his foundation for this, what is the basis of his knowledge? He comes into the situation at a particular point so at months, which place, what events. If we could take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question was very limited to the witness's dealings with Mr. Pusic during the period just prior to and just after the Washington agreement. So let us say end of December, January, February, the witness will talk about dealings and agreements with Mr. Pusic in March as well. In addition, the witness has testified about his dealings with others in the HVO in October 1993 and I expressly asked the witness about that so I think the foundation has been laid and the Trial Chamber and counsel are obviously free to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He asked about a policy. That's what caught my attention first of all, and I believe there is a lack of foundation. He can talk about what his dealings were with a particular individual or individuals at a particular time but now to ask about a policy of events such as "the taking of prisoners," that's his words, not mine, I'm not adopting them, unless he can lay a foundation, we are talking about a lot of events in a lot of different places. The gentleman does not have, at least to my knowledge, he doesn't -- he doesn't -- he lacks the foundation at this point. It's beyond his -- unless he can lay it through a series of questions, non-leading, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the witness is dealing with the HVO authorities about Muslim persons under their control. I think the witness is competent to testify about who those people are, they are the prisoners who have been taken, and the HVO policy in respect of releasing those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to make sure that I understand because now we're twisting it a little bit. We are talking about HVO policy of release. First it was HVO policy of taking and that's what drew my objection. I just want to make sure, what are we talking about? It was a compound question to start with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, would you reformulate your question? I follow the discussion where I think you referred to December 1993 going through to just before the Washington agreement, March 1994, and it's for that period that you wish the witness to provide the Court information you're talking about Mr. Pusic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you reformulate the question and relate it to a specific time period?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, witness, then the time period that I'd like to ask you about is the months of January, February, March and April of 1994, and my question first of all, I asked you about policy in respect of taking of prisoners. Let me ask it this way: Based on your dealings with Mr. Pusic and the HVO, as well as your experience with the HVO in the October 1993 release that you testified about, what was the general composition, who were the prisoners, in the camps, in the custody of the HVO? Were they civilians, were they soldiers, were they both? What can you tell us about the nature of the Muslims who are referred to by Mr. Pusic in the exhibit? Muslim -- persons of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to talk about politics and policy. I'm going to tell you about practice, the practice that I witnessed, and about what Mr. Pusic told me personally not only me but the representatives of the international community as well, including the ICRC. And Mr. Pusic said the following: "All men between 18 and 65 years of age are soldiers, and they should all be in camps or prisons." And that practice, and I had an opportunity of checking that out by talking to hundreds and hundreds of prisoners who had been released from camps in Herzegovina, in particular, that practice was implemented. That is to say, people were 18 to 65, but not only them. In the prisons, there were boys or young boys who were not yet 18. And there were those who were over 65 years of age. So that was the practice that was applied. The second practice that was partially successful, partially, which Mr. Pusic implemented and advocated publicly, was this: He maintained that all Croatians who lived on the territory not under HVO control were potential prisoners and that it was his task to see that those people were transferred from that territory, the territory where they were potential prisoners, to territory under the control of the Croatian Defence Council. So that practice too in countless cases was implemented. Sometimes the local authorities allowed this to take place. Sometimes they did not. And I'm talking about the local authorities in this case on territory under BH army control, with the proviso that the status of those categories of those civilian persons depended from case to case. It differed from case to case. The vast majority of them were in their own homes, in their houses, in their apartments, but there were other cases where those civilian persons were not in their own homes. They were not in their own flats. They were in some refugee centres and there were also cases and I have to say that quite openly, be quite frank, that some of those civilians were also deprived of their liberty and that was at the level of incidents that took place. So there were cases where a civilian would be captured without any legal basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me take you back to the first point you just raised, which was the practice of -- or the view that all the Muslim males between the ages of, I believe you said 18 to 65, are prisoners. That practice, then, when it was implemented and they were arrested, when it came to release, did that raise any particular issues or dilemmas on the side of the Muslim negotiators such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pusic asked us for assistance in putting that kind of practice into effect, the principle of a one-for-one exchange. Now, in implementing agreements like that, what Mr. Pusic asked me personally to do was that we should release the persons who were in prison, HVO members, and in certain cases members of the Croatian army, whereas in return, on the principle of one-for-one, he would release the Bosniak individuals who were in this category of civilians ranging in ages between 18 and 65, who were incarcerated in camps or prisons held by the HVO. So for us in Sarajevo, for the government, for the Presidency, we were faced with a moral dilemma, whether to agree to release from prison an HVO member, for example, who had been captured, and in reciprocity to have a Bosniak released by the other side. Some international organisations such as the High Commission for Refugees, High Commission for Refugees, exerted direct pressure on the government in Sarajevo to undertake this type of exchange of, well, in inverted commas, POWs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This principle, one-for-one, we have been talking about this awful principle for sometime now. But can we clarify this? In the areas which were controlled by the ABiH, wasn't the same practice adopted? Wasn't it also the case that civilians were arrested, Croatians aged between 18 and 65 years old, and following that, all-in-all was implemented? This is a question that I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That wasn't the practice. That wasn't the rule. I said that there were incidents and cases like that where Croatians, civilians, without any legal grounds, were taken off, taken into custody and taken to prison. That happened sporadically, as incidents. But the rule that the government adhered to, as did the BH army, was that it was only the POWs who could be held in prison and could be exchanged in the sense of the Third Geneva Convention and those civilian persons of Croatian ethnicity who had been captured or rather who had been incarcerated for crimes that came under the republican laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised as crimes and that were brought into connection with the war conflict, however that law was not applied only to Croatian civilians. The law was also applied to all civilians regardless of their ethnicity and they were crimes that they had committed such as armed rebellion, for instance, refusal to be mobilised. Another case in point, illegal possession of weapons or explosives. So the kinds of criminal acts that everybody could be held responsible regardless of their ethnicity. So those are the two categories. And if we are speaking of -- people of Croatian ethnicities who were in the prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just -- and perhaps just one observation, Mr. President. I noticed that earlier he had talked about when the Croats are in -- are being detained, they are in refugee camps. When the Muslims are being detained, they are in prisons. The Croat men of military age which they had to serve they are civilians when they are captured where the Muslims of military age which they had to serve they are somehow treated as prisoners. I believe this deserves follow-up questions that should not be dealt on cross-examination but rather the Bench perhaps should elicit information from this particular gentleman. He seems to be making some rather interesting distinctions which fly in the face of logic and common sense not to mention the law that was applying at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, indeed. You will have noted that was the reason I asked my earlier question but Mr. Stringer I think will certainly come back to this and if necessary the judge will as well. It's now quarter to 4.00. We are going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, let me take to you a different exhibit now. It's toward the front of the binder, number 5945. This goes to the issue that was raised just before the break, 5945 is a -- it's an interview of Mr. Pusic that's published on the 19th of October 1993 in the publication "Slobodna Dalmacija" and I want to take you to one of the questions and Mr. Pusic's response to the question and ask you to give us your comment on that. I can't take you to the Croatian version, but I want to go to the fifth page of the English version, at the bottom, and the journalist is asking Mr. Pusic: "Have you been holding talks about the release of detained Croatian soldiers?" Were you able to find that part in the original language version? The question is: "Have you been holding talks about the release of detained Croatian soldiers?"

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the response that's given is Mr. Pusic indicates that they are negotiating the release of both civilians and captured Croatian soldiers, "At the moment the Muslim side does not consider the civilians prisoners but in my opinion, every civilian is a potential prisoner, if he is not free to go where he wants. "So at first sight, all these are irrelevant details which the Muslim side in almost all negotiations presents as its conditions knowing that we cannot agree to them, all with the aim of preventing the exchange of detainees." Now, this statement of Mr. Pusic's, is that consistent then with the views that he expressed in his dealings with you about who the prisoners are, how the prisoners are defined, at least in respect of the Croats, either civilians or soldiers, who were in the territory held by the Armija?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. What he said corresponds to what I have stated. However, the point is not Mr. Pusic's claim that they are all potential prisoners. Behind that statement, you can discern a very dangerous intention. And the intention was, and I've already spoken about that practice, that those civilians should be taken out from their places of residence and transferred from those territories where they were all alleged potential prisoners to be transferred to the territory under the control of the HVO. That was the intention, i.e., that was the common practice that was in place, based on this statement of Mr. Pusic that all of them were potential prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on the Muslim side, then, what was the Muslim policy in respect of these proposals to exchange all Croats for example, who were in the areas held by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because I don't know what were the policies of the side that you're referring to as the Muslim side. Such a side did not exist, as far as I know, in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can talk about the policies of the government that appointed me as the head of the commission for the exchanges of POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that was my question. What were the policies that you were implementing based upon the instructions you received from the government?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: My task was to participate in the negotiations about the exchange of prisoners of war and persons deprived of liberty, which implied a circle of individuals who found themselves in the prisons in the territory under the control of the government and those individuals had either been convicted or charged with a limited number of crimes stipulated by the then-law that could have been considered to be in connection with the armed conflicts as it is defined in the agreement dated 1st October 1992, which was reached in Geneva, at the time when there were still no large-scale conflicts between the BiH army and the Croatian Defence Council. In other words, that agreement in Geneva provided for the release of prisoners of war and civilians who were imprisoned in connection with the crimes that had to do with the war conflicts. That was the policy of the government in Sarajevo as well as the policy that I was duty-bound to implement in practice when I was involved in the exchanges of POWs and persons deprived of freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was it the policy of the government that all males between the ages of 18 and 65, who were of Croat or non-Muslim ethnicity, that all such males would be arrested and held by the Armija for exchange purposes?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I don't know how is it possible to state something like that, given the well-known facts that such individuals of non-Bosniak ethnicity throughout the whole period of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were hundreds of thousands of such individuals residing in the territory under the control of the government forces. In Sarajevo alone we are talking about over 60.000 such people. In Tuzla as well, in Zenica, in Bihac and in other towns and settlements that were under the control of the government throughout the aggression. If this were true, if that policies were in place, all those people would have found themselves in prison, which did not happen. And the best proof of that are the reports of the International Committee of the Red Cross which had access to the prisons and camps, if we are talking about the Serb forces and partly about the Croatian Defence Council. In order to illustrate my words I'm going to give you some data. When it comes to the relationship between the BiH army and the HVO, the number of exhumed victims in the territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you that question in a little bit. We are going to be talking about the recent exhumation and I'm going to be asking you for some figures on that, Mr. Masovic, so let me just take to you that point in my outline by first going to Exhibit number 8084.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, before we move to that exhibit. I'm still with the interview given by Mr. Pusic. In this framework, he says that according to the reports he has available, 10.149 Croats are allegedly detained in the prisons of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and based on this figure, a question is put to him how many civilians are there, how many soldiers are there? And he says there are 3.149 soldiers. As for the remainder, they are civilians. So if I subtract that I have 7.000 Croat civilians who are detained by the Muslim side. What do you think of this? Are these figures exaggerated ones? Are they real figures? What do you have to say as to the figures mentioned by Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never ever, until this very day, did I see a list of prisoners, either prisoners of war or civilians that would show these numbers. None of the international representatives saw it either. And to be honest, I don't think that Mr. Pusic ever saw the list either. This list simply cannot exist because these names and family names simply do not exist anywhere. I would find it intriguing if such a list were presented during this trial, since there is a claim that it exist in the records. Quite the contrary: Throughout the conflict, the number of people missing, first imprisoned and then missing, and I'm talking about members of the HVO or Croatian civilians, according to the BiH army, never surpassed the figure of 1100, not for a single moment and I'm talking about the combined number of prisoners of war and civilians together. I'm also saying that the number of prisoners of war I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, but you're talking about potential prisoners, and the journalist asking the questions asks how many Croats there are that would be detained according to the ICRC records. And he answers, 850. What do you think of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I've just said. I started saying that a number of registered according to my information never surpassed the figure of 1100, and I believe that this corresponds with what Mr. Pusic said in the interview about the International Committee of the Red Cross figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: While we are on the Red Cross, let me take you to Exhibit 7852, 7852. Do you recognise this, sir, as a letter that was directed to you by the ICRC, the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the date of this letter is the 12th of February 1994 so this is getting close to the time of the Washington agreement. The second page of this exhibit contains numbers according to the ICRC of the number of Muslim prisoners who are detained as of this time; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My question is whether, in your view, the figures that were published or provided to the two parties, the two sides, by the ICRC tended to be in your view accurate or not accurate? Is this in your view a fairly accurate indication of the number of Muslim prisoners who were being held at this point?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is relatively correct, but I know for certain that subsequently, the ICRC registered in some of these places some other prisoners that were not on the original list, and I'm talking about Kiseljak, Livno, in Grude and Grude is missing from here completely, and I believe that the ICRC subsequently registered another prison in Grude whereas I don't see Grude as a prison here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit I wanted to take you to is Exhibit 8084. And while you're finding that exhibit, Mr. Masovic, I'll just say that what we are doing now is we are moving a couple of weeks after the Washington agreement, to the 17th of March 1994. You recognise this as an agreement that you and Mr. Pusic signed in respect of remaining prisoner releases to take effect after the Washington agreement?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise this. This is the Gornji Vakuf agreement dated 17 March 1994, which was signed by Mr. Pusic and myself in the presence of some witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 1.1 of that document, it provides that on the 19th of March 1994, a variety of prisoners will be released from different locations; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There is a reference -- there is a reference here to 73 prisoners from the prison in Mostar. Do you know who that is referring to? Which prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This refers to the prisoners that we have just discussed because of whom I went to Mostar in December 1993. They were members of the HVO and several members of the HV who had been imprisoned in East Mostar. They were one of the reasons for which the exchange process reached a stalemate at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the issue of getting release of those prisoners was never resolved until this time a couple weeks after the Washington agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has several times mentioned several prisoners of the HV. Can we have their names in order for us to be able to prepare until tomorrow and see who these people actually were and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you ask the witness? The problem is that Mr. Praljak says that he needs the names for cross-examination. He needs to know who these people are. Sir, you spoke about HV prisoners. We are talking about the Croatian army. How many of them were there? In this document you and Mr. Pusic signed, do we find an explicit mention of these HV prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are not mentioned in this document. If the fact that they were in the prison in East Mostar is in dispute, I can try and obtain their names before tomorrow. I can try. I don't know whether I will succeed. I don't know them by heart. If there is any dispute about the fact that they were members of the HV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... according to you, so were they members of the HV army who were imprisoned in East Mostar? How many? 10, 20? Five? Do you have any figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were prisoners in East Mostar, very few of them, maybe two or three altogether, and they were not the first members of the Croatian army that had been taken by the BiH army. Somewhat before that we had handed over the bodies of nine members of the HVO [as interpreted] who had been killed in an operation. They were handed over to Mr. Pusic at the local level. They were members of the HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My only observation would be that I know that General Praljak has excellent counsel and I'm sure they will be able to investigate that as well before tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The other part of this document that I wanted to take you to is paragraph 2.1 and it's just staying with the first paragraph 1.1, 1.1 is talking about a release of prisoners that is to take place simultaneously on the 19th of March; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 2.1, there is what appears to be envisioned a second round of releases that is to take place on the 22nd of March; is that correct? Is that how it was to work?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely so. That's how it worked. That's how it was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could ask my learned colleague to ask non-leading questions? This is a rather critical area. If we can just get a narrative so he can lay the foundation of what the procedure was, but for counsel to be leading and prodding this particular witness, who he's had several days at least to question and to proof, I don't think it's quite appropriate and the gentleman is a lawyer as well. He's a professional witness, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if I'm leading, I apologise. I think it's pretty self-evident I'm trying to keep things moving but we can ask the witness to describe what's being talked about in this paragraph. I'm actually mostly interested in the prisoners from Central Bosnia, Zepce, Novi Seher, Maglaj, Zenica and had intended to ask the witness specifically what he recalls about those prisoners who were at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it is written in the agreement, that's literally how it was implemented. So everything it says in the agreement was realised in the way in which it was written. I'm reading the provisions of the entire agreement and also speaking on the basis of my recollections and I think that each of the individual points including point 3 of 2 was implemented as the ICRC had stipulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then just to finish this document, 3.1 then makes a reference to a final exchange or release, I should say, that is to take place on the 24th of March. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It's a meeting, not release. We agreed to meet again on the 24th of March 1994 in Gornji Vakuf, in order to discuss the release of all the remaining prisoners of both sides. And I think that the meeting took place in Mostar, if I remember correctly, and that we didn't adhere to the letter of the agreement in that sense because it was in Mostar rather than what it says here but I'm not quite sure, but I think it was the 24th of March anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you remember what the issues were that were delaying the release of these prisoners who had come from the Central Bosnia areas?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The only reason, as far as I recall, was a certain lack of confidence and trust that prevailed between the two sides or between us as the heads of the commission, whether the other side would abide by what had been agreed and put it into practice, in view of certain previous agreements which had not been implemented and our experience there. So the only reason that I can remember is that quite simply we needed to see how the release would function of the 19th and 22nd of March so that the last stage of the release to be effected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this agreement then appears to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may in this context, does that mean that these prisoners from Central Bosnia were kept as some sort of a pawn, almost like hostages, by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to answer that question. We did agree to agreement like that, to developments like that. And my signature was placed on the agreement. I wasn't forced by anybody to sign it but I did sign it. That's what the agreement was like. And that's how we implemented it. Now, I can't remember in this particular case why it was that people from Central Bosnia were the last or amongst the last to leave Heliodrom, but I can just assume or guess at why that happened. The exchange was agreed at the level of Mostar, and the most important prisoners on both sides were from the Herzegovina area. So at a local level, in Herzegovina, it was important to pull the people out as soon as possible from that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What could have happened possibly, the number of people from Central Bosnia remained in the group of the last people to be released because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask whether on the other hand, and I don't find an answer in this document, whether the -- your side also had a certain reserve of prisoners that they with held for later release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That we held a certain number of prisoners? Well, there were a number of prisoners whom we released subsequently, and I think they were prisoners from the prison in Sarajevo and Zenica and possibly in some other places but those prisoners were left for the second stage of the release process. It wasn't the prisoners from Central Bosnia and Heliodrom held by the HVO. They weren't the only left-over prisoners in the conflicts between the BH army and the HVO. So the government, I think, had some ten or more prisoners in prisons in Sarajevo and Zenica and I think in Travnik as well, who were released in the subsequent stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic? Just a moment. Before we give Mr. Ibrisimovic the floor, can I just follow on from this question already raised? In paragraph 3.1, it states that on the 24th of March, there is to be a new meeting held because you sign a document on the 17th of March 1994. In paragraph 3.1, it states that there are still prisoners held in Central Bosnia by the HVO and by the ABiH but in paragraph 3.2, which has to be related to paragraph 3.1, it states that the HVO requests that there be a visit to Tarcin and Smijovic [phoen] in order to verify whether any Croats are being held in captivity in those locations. Isn't that actually the real reason for waiting one week to sort everything out? Since there were suspicions that there were people still being held in Mehurici and in Tarcin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that that's exactly how it was. So I was talking about a certain dose of mistrust between the representatives of the commission and Mr. Pusic already in Vakuf and I think that was recorded by the representative of the international community as well, he insisted upon the fact that the government was holding in some secret places a certain number of Croats, and he requested that the ICRC visit those so-called secret places. The international -- ICRC committee did that and reported back to us. They told us that there were no secret prisons or any new secret prisoners, so then we continued with the process of releasing prisoners overall.
