utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Might I be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and Mr. Masovic with regard to paragraph 2.2 and that is what the asked by Judge Trechsel was on, Catici and Vares were mentioned and that was under the BH army's control. Now, could the witness explain the status of Catici to us, please? And that will perhaps make it more understandable and the people who were in Catici as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 2.2, there is mention of three different locations. One of them was under the control of the Croatian Defence Council and that was called Rotilj. And it's a suburb of Kiseljak in actual fact, under HVO control. The other two locations mentioned are Vares, which at that time was under the control of the BH army. And it was specifically in Vares that 32 members of the Croatian Defence Council are mentioned who were released from prison there. So they were at liberty on the territory of Vares which was under the control of the BH army. Now, the third place that was mentioned is a place called Catici, that too was under the control of the BH army. Now what the status was of persons in these three locations should be looked at. Rotilj had an undefined -- they had an undefined status, their status was not clear. People that I interviewed who had left Rotilj claimed that they had been captured and held contrary to their own will, held in Rotilj. However, I think - let me repeat, I think - that the ICRC when it visited these people, did not record these people as having been captured, as persons captured, but as some individuals who found themselves in isolation and the ICRC used the term "isolated persons" referring to these people in Rotilj. So that was what I can tell you with respect to Rotilj. Now, Vares. Vares is what it says here, 32 former HVO members, had been taken prisoner and in keeping with the provisions of the Washington accords, were released from prison and later on they were able to move around and go where they wished. I think there were 30 or 31 of them who left the Vares territory and just one of them stayed on in the territory of Vares. Anyway, they were allowed to move around, they were given free passage and when they were transported from Vares, they weren't people who had been deprived of their liberty. Now the third group of persons were Croats, I think they were exclusively or almost exclusively civilians who happened to find themselves at the base of the French Battalion, the French Battalion's base in Catici. And that's what it says in this agreement, in the paragraph of this agreement that was signed by Mr. Pusic and myself. Now, if you want to ask me why they happened to be in the French Battalion base in Catici in the first place, my answer would be probably because they didn't feel safe and secure in their own homes near Catici or in Catici themselves where they lived. So they found themselves under UNPROFOR control and they were not individuals who had been captured or deprived of liberty, neither were they isolated persons as being isolated by the government forces. This agreement provided for the fact that for exclusively humanitarian reasons the problems of all these persons in Rotilj, Vares and Catici be resolved and that is what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So Mr. Masovic, then, just to bring this document to a close, I think you've indicated that to a quite a large extent, the agreement, the various items provided for in this agreement, were ultimately implemented and the prisoners were released in accordance with this agreement, certainly for the most part; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this agreement was implemented in its entirety, with the exception of the meeting in Gornji Vakuf, but that's not essential. It was to have taken place on the 24th of March but I think that actually it did take place but not in Gornji Vakuf but rather in Mostar, if my memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So there was resolution in respect of the 70 or the 73 HVO and HV soldiers that were one of the sticking points items from the beginning? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the question. What did you ask me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Initially, your initial involvement was in part related to the issue of the HVO --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes, yes, and my answer to your question is yes, this did resolve the problem of the 73 HVO and HV members. This agreement resolved that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now another issue you mentioned early on was the situation involving Mr. Demirovic and Mr. Mahmutcehajic. Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber whether this agreement or any other ultimately then resolved the issue of their release or their detention?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a form of political agreement, if I can put it that way, which took place between two presidents, Mr. Izetbegovic on the BH side and Mr. Tudjman on the Croatian side and then subsequently, after that, this was confirmed by the foreign ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, that is to say, Mr. Silajdzic and Mr. Granic, and I implemented it later on without the participation of my opposite number, Mr. Pusic, who was opposed to the agreement. The agreement was as follows: It said that two HVO members who had been arrested in Sarajevo because of having committed some crime of treason or whatever, because they were the commanders of a brigade, the commander and deputy commander of a HVO brigade in Sarajevo, Mr. Slavko Zelic and another deputy of his, I've forgotten his name just now. Anyway the agreement was that those two should be released and that the HVO on the other side shall release Mr. Mahmutcehajic as the top-ranking officer of the BH army held in captivity throughout the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, both between the Serb and Croatian side and Mr. Zijad Demirovic be released too. Now, I arrive with Mr. Slavko Zelic by UNPROFOR helicopter. I came to the confrontation line, if I can call it that, because the Washington agreement had already been signed but nonetheless there was still a check-point between the BH army and HVO south of Mostar in a place called Bisce Polje, I believe, and the other gentleman who was supposed in the helicopter with me refused to cross over into territory controlled by the HVO so he stayed on in Sarajevo and this created a fresh problem because after that, on the Croatian side, to all intents and purposes, the exchange was brought into question, according to the two-for-two principle. I was forced, from Mostar, to telephone Mr. Mato Granic and talk to him, as well as Mr. Bozic and Mr. Izetbegovic, as well as Mr. Silajdzic. I also had to talk to Mr. Pusic and contact all those people and I think some others too, Mr. Orucevic another one, and after a certain amount of trouble over a period of four or five days, Mr. Zelic was with me in Mostar but it was decided ultimately that the exchange should take place but that it would be two-to-one, that is to say, that the HVO should release Mr. Mahmutcehajic and Mr. Demirovic and that the government should release Mr. Zelic in view of the fact that this other member of the brigade command, the Kralj Tvrtko Battalion, refused to cross over into HVO-controlled territory and that took place on the 29th of March 1994. Two prisoners, Mr. Mahmutcehajic and Mr. Zelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, we are being asked to have you slow down just a bit for the interpreters and also the court reporters. I think actually you've brought us right to the end of that --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I finished what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to add was that Mr. Pusic did not attend the actual handover of these two prisoners. He was angry with me because allegedly, I had done this without his knowledge, worked without his knowledge, towards the release of Mr. Mahmutcehajic and Mr. Demirovic and the ICRC brought in the prisoners without the presence of the representatives of the commission or Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, your agreement with Mr. Pusic 19th of March or 17th of March, I should say, did that then result in resolution of the other sticking point which was the Vranica issue, the issue of the Vranica soldiers who had been captured and had gone missing on the 10th of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: When we drew up the agreement, I was conscious of the fact although I didn't have direct evidence of this, that 13 members of the BH army from Vranica were not alive and that in a way it would not be rational and not opportune or reasonable and wise to insist that they be released while holding all the other prisoners in camps and prisons belonging to the HVO. I didn't think that would be wise because of these 13 people to leave more than a thousand others in camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, we are now at a point in time that is after the Washington agreement so that the hostilities have for the most part ended and, as you indicated before, now the mission for you and for Mr. Pusic as well, I would think, changed, the focus of your work changed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Several other exchanges were to take place, the last taking place on the 21st of April, I believe, and then Mr. Pusic and I focused our attention on the second part of our mission, that is to say, to record and investigate the fate of all those who from the beginning of the conflict, that is to say from 1992 onwards, had disappeared or were missing and that nothing was known of their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So from this period, then, say, end of March 1994, going forward then into the years that followed the conflict, how many years, then, did you communicate, negotiate, with Mr. Pusic in respect of locating missing persons? How long did that relationship between you and Mr. Pusic continue after the conflict ended?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, our contacts more or less intensely went on for as long as Mr. Pusic was in the federal commission for tracing missing persons, and I think that was sometime in 1999, when Mr. Pusic, by the then-High Representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina, was replaced because of certain activities in another commission at state level, and that commission was called the commission for de-mining.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So during this then post-conflict period from March-April 1994 until the time that he was no longer involved in the missing persons, approximately how many times did you meet with him in respect of these issues of locating, finding missing persons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes those meetings were more intensive, sometimes less. We would meet in different places for different reasons, but I think that we met more than 60 or 70 times in all. We would meet on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and outside BH territory. Sometimes to deal with the problem of missing persons, sometimes we were parts of other delegations such as the central commission for missing persons. Then there was a joint military commission of some sort, and we were members of some other structures and organs where generals would meet or high-ranking officers who met from both sides to discuss some current problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber please the issue of the missing Vranica soldiers, how much of an issue did that remain in the months and the years immediately following the end of the conflict? How prominent an issue was that for you?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It was very important for the position that I occupied and the job I did because the problem was one that was a burden to our relations, to the two sides' relations, even after the establishment of peace, after the Washington agreements. Relationships particularly in Mostar were highly tense because of the problem of missing persons in Vranica and even while I'm testifying the problem still exists. It still hasn't been resolved. And even today, 14 years post festum after they had been captured and after they had gone missing it's still a problem for people on the east and west bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And why is this particular issue, these 12, what has, in your view, raised this to the issue of such importance or significance in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Their status is specific, if you compare the status of other prisoners or other prisoners who are missing. We have a list of missing persons made up by the International Red Cross committee, people registered in Heliodrom or some other camp, and we still haven't found those persons. We still have lists of them. But the problem of the 13 Vranica prisoners took on special significance because of the fact that the act of their having been captured was filmed, it was caught on camera. And then their families and their co-fighters and nearest and dearest or relations of theirs saw them being taken prisoner alive and this is footage that is frequently shown on Bosnian television stations to commemorate the anniversary of when they were captured, every 10th of May that footage is shown again and again. So that is why the problem is kept alive of those 13 prisoners. They weren't the only BH army members who were captured and went missing but that's why they take on such a lot of importance if you compare them to all the other events and incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Exhibit P 09036 is a short video clip that we've prepared. I think the same images are already in evidence. We think that this particular one is a bit better quality so we decided to use this one today, and I'll ask if we can just show the video segment that we've got and then I'm going to ask the witness some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, is that at least some of the video that you've just mentioned in terms of its having been broadcast in the -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely that footage. A shorter version of the whole tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, let me take you to your binder, Exhibit 8542. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: If this is a document called "Press release for the general public," this is not the document that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't think you have the right one, 8542.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I recognise this document. This is a document I drafted and signed and submitted to the families of the Vranica prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I think we should clarify at the beginning, because this document contains the names of 12 individuals, already in your testimony you've made reference to 13 prisoners. So could you clarify for the Trial Chamber, please, what the 12 comes from and what the number 13 then comes from?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: On the video footage that we just saw, you can see 12 members of the army captured in the Vranica building and that indeed was the case. 12 of them were captured in the Vranica building. The 13th person who is mentioned very often within the context of the Vranica building or the prisoners from the Vranica is Fedja Huskovic. He was indeed captured on the same day, also he was a member of the BiH army. His parents also resided in Mostar and his parents also joined the other parents, the other 12 sets of parents, of the prisoners, in order to raise the awareness of the international local public in order to help them and to learn about their destiny. However, that person was not captured in the Vranica building together with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And he's not on the videotape?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No. He does not appear on the videotape. And the moment of -- when he was captured was not recorded by a film camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct you to the very last sentence that you write in this certificate and ask if you could just explain what you're referring to here? What you're saying is that the explanations given by the HVO saying that some of those persons are currently abroad are not acceptable for the state commission. What are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: During my initial contact with Mr. Pusic, on the 29th December 1993, when I raised the question of the destiny of the 13 members of the army who had been captured in the Vranica building, Mr. Pusic told me something along these lines. Eight of them are alive. Ask Orucevic about their destiny. He was the one who exchanged them. At that moment, I didn't know how reliable that information was or wasn't. Obviously I got in touch with Mr. Orucevic as well as with some other people who were in Mostar involved in the process of exchanges. For example, the men called Safo Orucevic, Sefkija Djiho and Alija Alikadic, and they told me that this was not correct because none of them ever appeared alive, none of the 13 of them. In other words, when Mr. Pusic told me that Mr. Orucevic had exchanged those 8 of the 13 men from Vranica and sent them abroad this was obviously not accurate, and this is the intention of my last sentence in which I inform the parents' committee that the explanation given by the HVO saying that some of those persons are currently abroad are not acceptable to the state commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, and just so it's clear, you mentioned Mr. Orucevic; is that Mr. Safet Orucevic who was mayor of Mostar at the time?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pusic actually told me, ask Safo Orucevic about the destiny of these people. He'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next Exhibit is 8565, 8565. Now, Mr. Masovic, if I could just direct your attention to the bottom, if you recognise the signature down there at the bottom of this communique, tell us what this document is and who has signed it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The document was signed by Mrs. Azra Penava, I suppose. She was Fahir Penava's wife. This is a communique for the public which followed at the local level in Mostar after the session of the Presidency of the municipality of Mostar. At the session, the problem of the 13 prisoners from Vranica was discussed amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this person, Azra Penava, she's just so we are clear, can you tell us again who is she is? The record isn't quite clear on that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Penava was the wife of one of the 12 members of the BiH army who had been captured on the 10th of May and who appeared on the video footage that we have seen today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask you -- well, does she play any particular role in respect of all of the families of these missing soldiers from the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I would say that all of them together played a very important role throughout all that time because they put pressure on the authorities, which unfortunately did not bear any results. They have not stopped putting that pressure for 14 years now. I personally have received over a hundred letters from the Amnesty International organisation, from various countries, from various continents, and in all of these letters, the representatives of the Amnesty International have been inquiring about the destiny of the 13 army members from the Vranica building. Obviously I have never been able to tell them much, but that we are still trying to find what their destiny is but without any success. Mrs. Penava was the head of that committee and she was the most active member of the -- that committee. She has been the most active member of the committee for 14 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Exhibit 8595. It's the next one in the binder. This is dated the 17th of August 1995. Do you recognise this as a letter from Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to the letterhead and the signature, this will be the letter that Mr. Pusic sent to the office of the ombudsman of the federation in reference to the disappearance of three men that he mentions here, they were members of the BiH army. One of them was from the group of 12 from Vranica. The third person on the list, Fahir Penava. Fedja Huskovic is also mentioned among the 13 but he's not in the footage. And also Fadil Djelilovic [phoen] is mentioned, and he is one of the persons of whose destiny I don't know anything at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I wanted to direct your attention down below that. There is a reference to BH army general Jusuf Prazina, nicknamed Juka. And I wanted to then ask you to -- whether you, in any of your conversations with Mr. Pusic or whether Mr. Prazina's name has come up with connection with these prisoners from the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't mention him but Mr. Pusic often mentioned Mr. Prazina as a -- the person who allegedly was familiar with the destiny of the 13 members of the BH army from Vranica. He repeated it on several occasions, even before the letter sent to the ombudsman and later throughout all the time while Mr. Pusic was active in the commission for the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know who this person, Jusuf Prazina is? Was he a member of the ABiH or do you know his status?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prazina was the commander of one of the local units in Sarajevo of the BiH army for a while, and then because of some things that bordered on crime or were considered to be criminal acts, the way was found for him to be demobilised and to leave Sarajevo. After that, at least this is what was speculated at the time, he was outraged for having been expelled from the army and allegedly he joined the units of the Croatian Defence Council. I know that there were some problems for a while, that he held a point south of Jablanica, that people were robbed there, travelling from Mostar to Sarajevo, and then rumour had it that he had joined the units of the HVO. I don't have any direct information. I am speaking from the knowledge that I gained from the media and from what I heard on the grapevine in Sarajevo at the time. After the war, allegedly, he was killed in a showdown somewhere in Western Europe, I believe in Belgium but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall having a conversation with Mr. Pusic about the Vranica prisoners that took place in Geneva or I should say in the area of Geneva, Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that conversation. This was one in a series of conversations about Vranica which had taken place before Geneva and after the meeting in Geneva. Mr. Pusic, myself and several others --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Forgive me, let me just ask a couple of questions that lead up to this. Tell us, first of all, when did this particular meeting take place? Do you recall the month and the year, the date?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pusic and I were in Geneva between 16 and 21 July 1997. In Geneva or in the vicinity of Geneva. During the meeting of the working group of the International Committee of the Red Cross for the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Had you and Mr. Pusic been participating in a series of meetings of this working group?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were both active representatives in that working group and we both participated in its work. There were the so-called active representatives and observers. Mr. Pusic and I were in the ranks of the active participants, i.e., the representatives of the working group for the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then in the course of this series of meetings in Geneva, you had a conversation with Mr. Pusic about Vranica, the Vranica prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: As for the conversation about the prisoners from Vranica, there was such a conversation but not in Geneva. This was during the period between the 16th and 21 July 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Why don't you just tell the Trial Chamber then about the meeting where it took place.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: On the last day of the 11th meeting of the International Red Cross, i.e., the working group in Geneva, the ICRC organised an excursion for all the participants in the meeting. We were taken to the Geneva Lake and we were also taken to Montreux. It was and the 20th of July 1997. Mr. Pusic and I were talking on the lake in -- near the monument to Freddie Mercury, the frontman of the Queen band. Mr. Pusic had a very interesting proposal for me. He told me literally that he was prepared to give 16 members of the BiH army from Vranica should I give him 21 Croats who had been captured in Bugojno by the government forces and who had gone missing after having been captured. They were taken from the prison and nothing further was known about their destiny. At that moment, this was a surprise for me because this was the first time a reference was made to 16 prisoners. Before that, the reference was always made to either 12 or 13 prisoners. The first time ever Mr. Pusic mentioned the figure of 16 which I was not clear on at first, and later on, on reflection, I suppose that he wanted to strike a balance between the 16 members of the army and 21 members of the HVO from Bugojno because he might have thought that this would have been the way for him to learn about the destiny of those members of the HVO. I did not pay too much heed to that offer. I immediately replied that I would try and investigate although I knew even at that moment that it would be very difficult or impossible for me to obtain any information about these persons from Bugojno because already at the time it was almost certain that none of them had survived and that after having been taken from the prison, they were actually killed and the place where they were buried is not known. At that moment, already, I knew that I could not and I wasn't able to accept that proposal by Mr. Pusic but I promised I would investigate. After that I did not pay too much attention to that proposal, i.e. 16 for 21 because I believed at that moment that it was not a serious proposal on the part of Mr. Pusic. I did not take that proposal seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. In respect of these prisoners, these are HVO prisoners from Bugojno, correct? To this day do we know the fate of those men?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly nothing is known about the destiny of those 21 men who had been in the prison and taken from it. It is absolutely certain, after 14 years, that they are no longer alive. My colleague, Marko Jurisic and I tried to investigate. We went to six or seven different locations including a diving team that did a search in a lake near Bugojno. We followed a trace. We were digging. We had contacts with the alleged perpetrator of a crime against these people. Unfortunately, all this was to no avail and to this very day, I am not aware of their destiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At this meeting in which Mr. Pusic discussed these Vranica prisoners with you, was anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague from the commission who was in charge of the Mostar region, her name was Sanja Mulac, she was nearby. Later on, I tried to talk to Sanja Mulac about that and she was equally surprised when she heard Mr. Pusic's proposal mentioning a total of 16 members of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me take you to the last document, the last exhibit in the binder, number 10354. Do you recognise that exhibit, Mr. Masovic?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photo which was taken on the 19th of July 1997 in Geneva as we were leaving for a dinner party organised by the International Red Cross for the participants of the 11th meeting of the working group for the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you recognise Mr. Pusic in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pusic is the first on the left in this photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the person next to him?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The person next to him is Mrs. Sanja Mulac, the head of the office for the missing persons in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then are you in that photo as well?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I am the fifth person in the photo, from left to right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Masovic, I'd like to move forward now some ten years and ask you whether you recall hearing of a potential or a mass grave site in the area between Mostar and Siroki Brijeg in the month of May 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could Mr. Masovic maybe identify the other people depicted in the photo? I don't think that that should be a problem. He has identified Mrs. Mulac, himself and Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can indicate the names of the other persons that are on this photo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to the names that I've already mentioned from left to right, Mr. Pusic, Mrs. Mulac, Mr. Perkovic, the lady from the ICRC, I believe her name is Margaret. Then myself. I don't know the name of the next person but I know that she was a member of the local Red Cross, i.e., the Red Cross of Bosnia-Herzegovina based in Sarajevo. And the last person is Mrs. Fadila Mujic, a member of an association of the family members of the persons missing from Srebrenica. She was a member at the time. She no longer is. At that time she was in charge of one of the Srebrenica associations of the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, then, bringing you back to my last question, in May of this year, did you or your colleagues with the commission hear of a grave site that had been located or potentially located in the area between Mostar and Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th May of this year, Mrs. Mulac called me from Mostar to inform me that an exhumation was underway of a number of victims in a location near Mostar on the Mostar-Listica-Siroki Brijeg road. The exhumation was carried out by our colleagues from Republika Srpska, i.e., from a different entity. Mrs. Mulac believed at the time that among the victims there were no Serbs or at least that's what she had been told when she arrived in the location, but rather that the victims in the mass grave were actually of Bosniak ethnicity. After that, I told Mrs. Mulac that I would turn up on the following day, on the 18th of May, in the location of that exhumation, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that on the first day, the 17th of May, this is an exhumation that was being undertaken by representatives of the Republika Srpska. Why is it that people from the RS, then, would have been out at this location west of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The source that helped to locate the mass grave claimed that the victims in the grave were Serbs. I believe that he even said that there were between seven and 12 bodies in the grave, and that they had been killed on either the 14th or the 15th of June 1992 near Mostar in a neighbourhood called Podvelezje. Governed by the agreement on the inter-entity exhumations that stipulated that the exhumation should be carried out by the entity for which it was considered that the victims belonged to, and in this case the victims were believed to be the Serbs, then the Republika Srpska contacted the competent prosecutor in order to undertake the exhumation. That's why Republika Srpska turned up in Western Mostar. Had we had information that the victims were either Bosniaks or Croats, in that case, the exhumation would have been carried out by my commission, i.e., the federal commission for the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll just continue. I'm not sure what the breaking point is. I can continue for a couple minutes, I think, and move through a couple exhibits rather quickly with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, let me then ask you to turn to Exhibit 10322. And I'll venture perhaps to ask a couple questions that could be possibly perceived as leading in order to move a little more quickly through this. I know that counsel can and will object if they think I've crossed the line. Mr. Masovic, is this an exhumation report that was made by the authorities of the Republika Srpska dated the 17th of May 2007?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report that was compiled by the district prosecutor's office and district prosecutor, Mr. Salvarica [phoen] from the district Prosecutor's Office in Trebinje in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now, it appears to me to be the fourth name down. Is that a reference to Ms. Mulac, your colleague whom you've already referred to in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is Mrs. Sanja Mulac, representative of our commission from the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So her name is not spelled correctly there but that is who we are talking about. And was she then present at the site when the exhumation was carried out on the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In the original document, her name is properly written and spelled, Sanja Mulac. In the English translation there is a mistake. It says Mulic, it should be Mulac, but her name is properly written in the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: But she was present and as I said a moment ago, she contacted me that day and informed me that she considers that the victims were Bosniaks since certain traces of their uniforms were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then the next exhibit is 10323. And then is this the exhumation report then for the following day, the 18th of May 2007?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the exhumation report. This time compiled by the main prosecutor of the district Prosecutor's Office in Trebinje. Her name was Slobodanka Gacinovic and she did so on the 18th of May 2007 after the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And were you present then yourself at the exhumation site on the 18th of May?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I see that on the second page of the translation, third name down, it appears they've misspelled your name but I think we determined yesterday that your name is not correctly spelled in the original document either.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Not in the original document or in the translation is my name written properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, just one last question before the break. I think it's useful to raise this now before we go into greater detail. This exhumation then and the events that followed, has that all resulted in final official determinations regarding the remains and the identities of the remains, the victims found, at this location?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The interpretation I heard does not end in a question mark, as a question, so I'm not sure what you actually asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We are going to be looking at a series of documents that relate to the subsequent work done on the remains found at this site. My question is: Are any findings on all of this final and official as of this point in time?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Everything that was ongoing and done after the exhumation was official, but some of it wasn't final.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And that's my question: Have we made a final, official determination of the identity of all of the persons or victims whose remains are found at this location?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Let me say first of all that on location, 16 bodily remains from found, incomplete, of the victims so none of these 16 victims have been completed. There are bodily parts missing or parts of the skeleton that are missing. But for 15 of those 16, a preliminary identity has been set used DNA methods of identification. But we still don't have the identity of one of those victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And because these are preliminary DNA findings, I just want to sort of flag this for everyone, I'm not going to be asking you about some of the items found at the site such as watches, rings, things of that nature which relate to identification issues related to family members. We are only going to talk about the DNA results; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before -- the gentleman can answer the question. I assume they prepared him in the back. But before he answers any questions with respect to DNA, I suspect they are going to have to lay a foundation. If he's here merely to say this is the report that was handed to us, certainly we don't need the gentleman. It doesn't mean that the DNA results, if they are results, are accurate because that has to be brought in through an expert but certainly I would object to having this person turn into an expert to testify about DNA evidence when in fact, at least as far as I know, he's an advocate, he's a lawyer. Maybe on the side he's gone to medical school or he's got some other degrees in science.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could go to private session I could tell the Chamber where I'd like to go and where I don't want to go with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have 45 minutes remaining, Mr. Stringer by which time you should try to conclude. You've used two hours and seven minutes already.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, at the time that we took the break, you were looking at Exhibit P 0 -- I'm sorry, P 10323 which is the exhumation report dated 18 May 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I think you indicated that you were then present at this site called the Goranci site on that day?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, the second day of the exhumation, the locality is called Prikinac – Prikinac, the microlocation is the Rimski Bunar or Roman well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, in general terms, the extent of your experience as the commissioner or as a director of the commission on missing persons, your experience on this process that begins with an exhumation and then carries through DNA testing ultimately to identifying the victims for their families? How experienced are you in that process and what is the actual level of participation? What is it that you do?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the process of identification itself, I have been engaged in that for more than 15 years now, since 1992, October of that year, when I attended the identification of a body -- of bodies which were handed over to the commission whose vice-president I was for purposes of identification in an exchange, up until 2000, the identification of witnesses was conducted by using the classical method, the method of recognising the victim by close family member.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I just want to make sure we have got the record is correct. I'm seeing the English translation or the English transcript that you are talking about the identification of witnesses. I think --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. Victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- Identification of victims is what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said identification of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then, since the year 2000, how did the method of identification change?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Arriving on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, the international commission for missing persons, which established special laboratories for DNA identification in Tuzla, launched the process of identification using the DNA method. And by comparing the blood samples taken from the surviving family members of the missing persons and by comparing them to the skeletal remains or the DNA structure obtained from the skeletal remains of the exhumed victims. If matching takes place, or rather, if the DNA from the blood sample and from the skeletal remains is the same, then we say we have a positive match and that means that we have identified the victim preliminarily, and that was the case with the 15 exhumed victims from the Goranci grave site. After the DNA analysis, and after obtaining a positive match, we undertake the process of a final identification, and that is done in the following way: The matching DNA results are put to the family members, they are shown to them, as relating to a specific victim and then ante-mortal and post-mortal information is compared and checked once again, the height of the victim is looked into, the age of the victim, any clothing that was present, and might be recognised by a family member, or some personal objects, personal effects, such as pens, lighters, watches, items of jewellery or anything else. And then the family members try and identify those objects and items and match them to the victims. Once this entire process has been completed, a minutes is compiled, a report on the identification of the victim, and a family member, close family member, signs the report and then the bodily remains are available to the families for burial. The procedure is such that the DNA samples taken from the victims are taken by a local forensic expert or forensic expert working pursuant to instructions from the prosecutor and he takes one or if need be more DNA samples, if we are dealing with victims that are not compact, as in the Goranci site grave, which is a secondary grave site. The bodies of the victims were completely decomposed. Some of the -- some parts of the skeleton are missing and they probably remained in the primary location where the victims were buried first. And that primary location is unknown to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Since you've come back to this particular site, let me ask you about that. Do you know from this particular site how many bones or artifacts are missing, that is, not found at this site?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] ... ribs or vertebrae.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you could just start your answer again. We stopped getting the interpretation there. The question was, yeah, if you know, how many bones or artifacts are missing from this site?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to give a precise number of skeletal parts that are missing. But we estimate that it's more than 50, more than 50 bones are missing, from the 16 victims. Mostly they are small bones that are missing, such as finger bones, bones of the fingers, hands, feet, ribs, vertebrae. Some parts of larger bones such as the upper arm or lower arm. And especially parts of the skull are missing, with these victims, which once again indicates that those skulls were damaged and destroyed either when the victim was liquidated or when the victims were transported from the primary site to the secondary site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do object to this testimony. He's not -- unless there is a foundation that he is an expert where he's now talking, he's giving expert opinion. Now, they've had experts. Have the experts determined that there was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the Chamber always listens very closely to what you're saying but the witness has worked in this area for 15 years. I don't think anybody else is better positioned to talk about this subject. Sir, could I ask you a question of my own? For the last 15 years or so you've been working in this area. Have you been involved with Srebrenica, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe just one sentence will suffice to provide the entire explanation. I'm probably the one who has attended the higher number of exhumations or identifications than any expert witness in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why is that? Because the expert witnesses focus on the work of one court in very narrow area, the area of my activity is Prijedor, Srebrenica, Zvornik, the entire state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and neighbouring states so I believe that I have a lot of experience and that I can talk about whether a skeleton is complete or incomplete after exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He is testifying as an expert we haven't been noticed that he's an expert witness. So I object. If he's testifying that he has some background information, again, I don't think that he's qualified but if he's testifying as an expert, he is not been brought here as an expert witness. We have no notice and I would object to him testifying on -- as that because now he's claiming to be an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please carry on, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm running short of time so I'm going to keep marching on and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me just, on the last point, Mr. Masovic, do you have an idea in general how many exhumations have been carried out under the auspices of the commission for which you've been the commissioner or the director? How many exhumations are you responsible for in your years?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Over 370 mass graves, the graves containing five plus victims. Over 2.000 individual graves. Over 18.000 victims, including the Srebrenica victims, is something that my commission has been involved in. In other words, over 18.000 victims were exhumed as part of the mandate of my body over the past 11 years. Over 15.000 victims have been identified of the 18.000 that have been exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, let me -- I want to take you quickly through a series of exhibits here and ask you just to tell us very briefly what they are, whether you recognise them, and then we will come back and I'll ask you some more general questions about them. So if you would turn to Exhibit 10337? Again, just for the technical booth, this is the -- we are getting into the evidence now that we are going to be asking be put under seal. Witness, can you just take a look at this and tell the Trial Chamber what this is or what these three documents are that are in this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: These are the three so-called positive matches, i.e., three confirmations that the skeletal samples which were taken from various parts of one body belong to one and the same person, and based on the comparison with the blood of the surviving family members, it is confirmed with a degree of certainty of 99 and -- 99 thousand 99 [as interpreted] that this person is Camo Alija. And that he was a member of the BiH army who had been captured in the Vranica building and one of those that we had occasion to see on the video footage. In this specific case we are talking about the upper jaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Masovic. I really apologise for cutting you off but I'm going to move on so that we can cover all 15 of these very briefly just so that we are attending to all of them. So you've just mentioned Mr. Camo Alija as being in this Exhibit 10337. One question about these reports, these DNA reports, are these the types of reports that come to you in the normal course of your work on the commission and then dealing with the families?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a copy of the original report which is typically submitted to the forensic expert who takes the bone samples from the victim and then he submits the report to the competent prosecutor's office and to us as a commission in order to enable us to get in touch with the victim's family and inform them that we have a positive match, i.e., a positive identification. In other words, that it had been established through the DNA analysis that the victim is their potential relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now turning to Exhibit 10338 can you tell us who these results pertain to?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: These results pertain to Mr. Senad Cehic. Again we have several DNA analysis results in several samples were taken from the body, Senad Cehic is also one of the captives from Vranica that we saw on the video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then 10339.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, the victim who was preliminarily identified is Dzevad Colic, also a member of the Vranica group. He was also identified on the video footage that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now when you say preliminarily identified, now, what exactly does that mean?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I've just explained that this means that the family will be informed, in this particular I've already informed all the families in the case of the Goranci mass grave. The family has been informed about the positive match and the families have to prepare for the final act which is the signing of the record on identification of the victim after which the victim will be handed over to the family who will then determine the date, the place where the body will be buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Next is 10340.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mimo Grizovic, confirmation that we had a match between the skeletal remains and the blood samples provided by his mother and his father. He is also one of the victims seen on the Croatian television video footage depicting the capturing of the Vranica group.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vahidin Hasic, a confirmation that that indeed was him, based on comparing the blood samples of his mother and his father and the skeletal remains which were taken from his body, another from the Vranica group depicted in the video footage.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Dzevad Husic. In this case, the blood sample was taken from his father and his sister. We had a positive match based on the DNA method. He's also one of the Vranica group that were depicted in the video footage.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Zlatko Mehic, the blood sample was taken from his mother and his father. We had a positive match, again this was a long-haired young man in boots with hands in his pockets on the video footage, one of the Vranica group as well.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Nenad Milojevic, the blood sample taken from father and mother, there was a positive match, also he was featured on the video footage in the Vranica group. In this case his mother was also given an object that was found by the mortal remains that she was able to identify. The object was the young man's ring.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fahir Penava. Blood was taken from his wife, his daughter, his son and his mother and we had a positive match, i.e., confirmation that this was preliminarily identified Fahir Penava, one of the Vranica group featured in the video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's the wife of Mr. Penava, Azra Penava is the one you spoke of earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next is 10346?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nazif Sarancic. Blood was taken from mother and father, positive match by the DNA method. One of the Vranica group from the video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 10347? Before we talk about this next one then, Mr. Masovic, so far, we've been talking about soldiers who were identified in the Vranica footage. Now, these next five, what can you tell us about those?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: What can I -- what I can tell you with certainty is that all the prisoners that were featured on -- in the video footage of the Croatian television were not preliminarily identified by the DNA method and it is absolutely certain at the moment that two of the 12 were not found in the mass grave in Goranci. As for the remaining six who were exhumed, in addition to the Vranica group, five were identified. One victim's identification is still pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, of the Vranica group and the 12 on the video as well as the 13th, then we do not have an identification for Hasan Balic, Selfko Pobric or Fedja Huskovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Not only do we not have their positive identification but it is also abundantly clear that their bodies were not in this mass grave because the blood taken from their family members did not match any of the DNA samples taken from the skeletal remains. So we are absolutely certain that they were not in that group of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, these remaining five whose remains or parts of their remains were found, is there anything in general that you can tell the Trial Chamber about these individuals in terms of where they were last seen or their status as missing persons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: We provided a laboratory with a total of nine names of whom we knew that they had gone missing between the 9th of May which was the beginning of the conflict in the Mostar region and the 13th of May which was the date that we noticed on the watch of one of the victims. We submitted the names of nine names and of those names, the laboratories. By way of DNA methodology. Established that they were from that group, Sabit Askraba, Hamza Filipovic, the Drace brothers, Alica and Dragan Drace, and Esad Husic. Those were the five names. All of them save for one whose status is not clear, but four of them at the moment of disappearance were members of the army who did not go missing in combat. It is certain that the Drace brothers, Alica and Dragan, had been taken from Alica Drace's apartment, one of the brothers' apartment, and it was either the 10th or the 11th of May. In any case, all five of them had been reported as missing in the period between the 9th and 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the record, Mr. President, the tests for Sabit Askraba are at Exhibit 10347. Those for Alica Drace are at 10348. Those results from Dragan Drace are at 10349. The results for Hamza Filipovic are at 10350. And finally, the results for Esad Husic are at 10351. Now, Mr. Masovic, if I could just take you quickly back, you could perhaps inform the Trial Chamber of -- about Exhibit 10324. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this exhibit is, please?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This is photo documentation of the scene by the ballistic expert, a member of the commission for missing persons of Republika Srpska based in Banja Luka. He is their permanent member. Upon his arrival at the location of the mass grave, he took some 150 photos starting with the situation that he found at the site and then in the course of the exhumation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we did not load all these photos into e-court just because it takes so much space and it takes a long time to bring them up so rather than using the ELMO for them, I think I'll just leave it at that, unless the Trial Chamber has any specific questions about any of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do actually have a question for you, sir, Witness. I'm looking at photo number 1 which indicates a field with some bushes, that type of thing. Photo 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. And that brings us on to the location of the bodies but earlier on you talked about a source that had indicated that there were Serbs that were buried. But in order for us to go to exactly the location as indicated on photo number 7, the source must have been indicated very, very clearly or precisely as to where was located the point where the bodies had been buried because otherwise, the situation is impossible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking based on my own experience in locating mass graves and I can claim with a high degree of reliability that without a witness who can identify the microlocation of the mass grave, it would be impossible, absolutely impossible, to identify the mass grave because there were no changes in the vegetation, in the configuration of the terrain. In other words, the mass grave would not have been identified if he hadn't brought our colleague from the commission of the Republika Srpska to the site and pointed the site to him precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I see that the photos are in e-court so they magically obtained them somehow. They're good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, one thing going back to the DNA testing, the preliminary results that now you've commented on, in the years that you've been involved in this process with the ICMP, do you know of any times when these preliminary DNA results have actually turned out to have yielded an incorrect identification? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently Mr. Praljak has not heard what's been said apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't think the witness heard me either. I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, my question was whether in all the years that you've been involved in this process with the ICMP, do you know of any times when these preliminary DNA results have actually turned out to have yielded an incorrect identification?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I have to say that the laboratory in Tuzla has carried out over 10.000 preliminary identification through the DNA analysis for the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Kosovo, for the entire area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia and Kosovo. We marked the 10.000th DNA identification recently and not a single one of them proved to be incorrect. It is impossible actually. The DNA analysis has served us to correct some mistakes that we made up to the year 2000 in the course of the so-called classical identifications. The DNA analysis has helped us to correct some misidentifications through the recognising of the clothes, the effects, which were wrong, and now I'm not aware of a single case, either from Kosovo, Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, that led to a wrong conclusion, that the DNA analysis identified one person and then subsequently something else proved the preliminary identification wrong. We simply have not had such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And my final question is this: And you've mentioned this issue of a secondary site, and I know that you're not an expert and that it's for others to conclude whether or not in a formal official way this is a primary or secondary site so let me just ask you about the issue in general, say, for example, Srebrenica. Have you had experiences in dealing with remains that have been found in secondary sites in connection with Srebrenica and other exhumations?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my experience with some locations in the municipalities of Prijedor and Srebrenica, but the cases of secondary mass graves were even more drastic, for example, in Srebrenica, where we have a victim whose body was found in four different locations and the distance between the four of them is more than 30 kilometres. In other words, when his body was moved from the primary grave, the excavators and the lorries that transported those skeletal remains and, mind you, those mass graves contained over 1.000 victims, simply transported the remains to four different graves. This person, a young man from Srebrenica, despite the fact that his remains were found in four different locations, this person's body is still not complete. Some parts of his skeleton are still missing and this is where the DNA method is very important because without the DNA method we would never be able to say that his body had been reburied in four different locations. Owing to the DNA analysis we are able to partially complete that body from the four different locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in terms of the process that takes place in which the families are identified, they are presented with the DNA testing results and other artifacts, could you then tell the Trial Chamber the impact on the families of these victims then when you have situations in which secondary grave sites are involved so that not all of the body parts, the remains, can be recovered? How does that impact this whole process?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about a primary mass grave, this implies that the bodies are complete and for the family, this is the end of their personal agony. They stop suffering the uncertainty, the pain that is connected with that which lasts for a decade in certain cases. When it comes to the secondary mass graves, and Goranci will probably be one of them because a lot of the skeletal remains are still missing, the families agony continues even after the identification is completed. Why? When the families recognise the ten victims from Vranica, when we hand over the mortal remains to them, when these mortal remains are buried and when after their graves there are tombs -- above their graves, there are tombstones, this is still not the end of the agony for their family because we, after having located if we ever do, the primary grave, in that grave we will again find parts of the same victims, the same ones that had already been handed over to the families and we will again have to knock on the doors of the same families and inform them that we have actually located yet another bone or the -- a part of the skull of their husband. In other words, the agony of these members whose dearest were buried in the secondary graves do not stop with the identification but they rather continue and go on and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Masovic. Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just add one very small question? Are there any efforts made when you have a secondary grave to find the primary one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm personally involved in that. I'm in contact with a source who brought us to the secondary location and we are trying to use that same source to get to the primary location but not only to the primary location but also to the mortal remains of the remaining three from the Vranica group for whom we are now certain that they are not in this particular mass grave, and we hope that we will succeed in our efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you have completed your leading examination. The counter-examination, the cross-examination will take place tomorrow. There will be no contact with the Prosecution. Over that period, you're now a witness before justice so tomorrow we will reconvene at 2.15. By the way on Wednesday and Thursday, we will be holding session in the morning starting at 8.00. So we'll recommence tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of November, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
